analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that let multinational corporations shift profits and jobs offshore.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2023 with 17 Democratic sponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise taxes on multinational corporations that move profits or headquarters offshore. It would tax foreign profits at the full rate instead of a reduced one, stop companies from blending low-tax-country profits with high-tax-country taxes to shrink their US bill, cap deductions for interest that let companies load debt onto US operations, tighten rules on corporations that reincorporate abroad to escape US taxes, and tax foreign companies that are actually run from the United States as if they were US companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit because multinationals would report more income in the US, shrinking the deficit or reducing pressure to raise taxes elsewhere. Domestic workers and communities benefit because the tax code would no longer reward companies for locating profits and operations abroad. US companies that keep operations at home would compete on a level field against rivals that shift income offshore.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the reduced tax rate on foreign profits of US multinationals, so income earned through foreign subsidiaries is taxed at the full corporate rate [S2][S3].
Requires the foreign tax credit to be applied country by country, so companies can no longer mix profits from tax-haven countries with taxes paid to high-tax countries to cut their US bill [S2][S3].
Caps the interest deductions of US members of large international corporate groups, closing a common way companies move profits offshore by paying deductible interest to affiliates [S2][S3].

Tightens the rules on corporate tax inversions, treating foreign reincorporations as domestic if former US shareholders hold 80% or more or if the company is still managed from the US with substantial US business [S2][S3].

Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for income tax, and taxes foreign oil-related income currently under the anti-shelter rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: US-headquartered multinationals, oil and gas companies with foreign operations, corporations that reincorporated in low-tax countries, and fund companies that manage assets from the US but are chartered offshore would all pay more tax, and highly leveraged multinationals would lose part of their interest deductions.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is complex: the country-by-country rules and financial-statement-based interest limits require detailed reporting that the Treasury Secretary must flesh out in regulations, adding costs for businesses of all sizes in multinational groups [S3].

Some provisions reach back in time: the tightened inversion rules apply to corporate transactions dating back to December 2017 and extend the window for assessing tax on those deals by three years, which can surprise companies that acted under the old rules [S3].

Raising taxes on US-headquartered multinationals can put them at a disadvantage against foreign-based competitors that are not subject to the same rules, and some of the added tax cost may be passed to consumers through prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the parts of the tax code that most reward keeping profits and operations offshore, and those breaks are real: the reduced rate on foreign profits, blended foreign tax credits, and interest-driven profit shifting all cost the US Treasury revenue. The main honest objections are complexity and retroactivity, which are design flaws rather than reasons the policy fails; the competitiveness concern is the strongest one, since a US-only tax increase can push some operations to foreign rivals rather than home.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, joined by 16 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it stayed for the rest of the 118th Congress with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US-headquartered multinationals, oil and gas companies, and corporations that reincorporated offshore keep the lower tax rates and deductions the bill would have ended, and the revenue those breaks cost the Treasury is never collected.

for.name: Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on the day it was introduced; the committee never held a markup or vote on it during the Congress.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it never came to a vote, so there is no roll-call record of bipartisan support.

industries.note: The bill removes the reduced rate on foreign profits and the blended foreign tax credit that let multinationals book income in low-tax countries at a fraction of the US rate, so they would owe billions more in US tax. That revenue currently falls on other taxpayers or the deficit.
Foreign oil-related income would become immediately taxable under the anti-shelter rules instead of escaping current US tax, closing a break long available to companies producing oil abroad.
Tighter ownership and management-and-control tests would treat many companies that moved their headquarters to low-tax countries as domestic again, restoring their US tax bill.

industries.industry: Offshore-chartered asset managers and fund companies
industries.note: Foreign corporations managed from the United States, including investment firms that run US investor money from a foreign legal domicile, would be taxed as US companies.
US members of large international groups would face a cap on interest deductions tied to the group's financial statements, limiting a technique for shifting taxable income out of the US through debt.
